passage:
Sit, Parveen, let me tell you something from when I was twenty-one. I'm Imran, and back then I was the commerce student in our friend group.

One evening four friends came to me. "You understand markets. Put our money together and invest it for us." I felt so flattered, like I was finally somebody. And underneath I felt a weight, because I knew I only understood a little from a few classes.

I didn't take it. I said, "I know less than you think. I won't hold your money, and I can't promise any returns. If you want to learn, I'll study with you."

One friend sulked for a month. But none of us lost anything, and he came back.

qa.q: How old was Imran when the friends asked to have their money invested?
What two feelings did Imran have when his friends asked?
qa.a: Imran felt flattered, as if finally somebody, and also burdened by a weight because he knew he understood only a little.

qa.q: What would you say to a young person asked to invest friends' money?
qa.a: Be honest about your limits, do not hold others' money or promise returns, and offer to study together or point them to a qualified adviser.

qa.q: How did the friends see Imran's refusal at first?
qa.a: One friend sulked for a month, probably feeling turned down after showing trust, but he came back once nothing was lost.

grounding: Friends want Imran to pool their money because he understands markets, and he admits his limits and refuses to hold money or promise returns.

passage: In Moga, everyone in Vinita's college group knew she read the business pages and had won the commerce olympiad in Class 12. So when Gurpreet and four others pooled their Diwali money, they came to her house with a steel box. 'You understand markets. Invest it for us. Just double it by next Diwali,' Gurpreet said, laughing, but the others were serious. Vinita felt flattered, and then heavy, as if the box weighed a hundred kilos. She pictured losing it, and five friendships with it. She pushed the box back gently. 'I read about markets. That's not the same as knowing. I can't take your money or promise anything back.' Gurpreet looked disappointed. 'You're the only one who knows this stuff.' 'Then let's all go to the bank's free investor session on Saturday. We can learn it together, instead of me guessing with your money.' Three of them came.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet and the others bring the money?
qa.a: They brought it to Vinita's house in a steel box.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel when asked to invest the money?
qa.a: Vinita felt flattered and then burdened, as if the box weighed a hundred kilos.
She was honest about her limits, refused to take their money or promise returns, and suggested learning together at the bank's session.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Vinita's refusal?
qa.a: Gurpreet is disappointed, seeing Vinita as the only one who knows this stuff.

grounding: Shows friends asking the one who 'understands markets' to run their pooled money, and Vinita honestly naming her limits and refusing to take their money.

passage: In the student flat in São Paulo, Siddiq had made a spreadsheet: six friends, each putting in a month's rent, and Priscila 'running the fund' because she was the economics student who had once explained interest rates at a party. 'You'll triple it,' he said. 'You know this stuff.' Priscila looked at the names, her flatmates, her study partner, her cousin, and felt a flush of pride, then a knot in her stomach. She had never managed anyone's money but her own, and even that badly last semester. 'Siddiq, I'm flattered. But I've studied theory, not handled real money. If I lost your rent, I'd lose you too.' 'You're being too modest.' 'Maybe. But I'm not taking anyone's money, and I can't promise anything back.' She opened her laptop instead. 'What I can do is show you the free course our faculty runs. We could all take it.' Siddiq sighed and deleted the 'fund manager' column.

qa.q: How much was each friend to put in?
qa.a: Each friend was to put in a month's rent.

qa.q: What did Priscila feel on seeing the names?
qa.a: Priscila felt a flush of pride, then a knot of worry in her stomach.

qa.q: What did Priscila offer instead of running the fund?
qa.a: To show them the faculty's free course so they could all learn, while refusing to take money or promise returns.

qa.q: How does Siddiq see Priscila at first?
qa.a: Siddiq sees her as the expert who will triple their money and thinks she is being too modest.

grounding: Shows friends trusting Priscila to run a pooled fund, her mix of pride and burden, and an honest refusal to take their money or promise returns.
